title: Sending Secrets Without Sharing a Secret First

sources.title: RFC 9180 — Hybrid Public Key Encryption
sources.notes: Introduces hybrid asymmetric/symmetric designs and KEM/KDF/AEAD composition. Episode distinguishes its conceptual wrapped-key teaching model from exact HPKE.

sources.title: RFC 5116 — An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption
sources.notes: AEAD confidentiality/integrity interface, authentication failure, and scheme-specific nonce requirements.

sources.title: RFC 8446 — TLS 1.3
sources.notes: TLS1.3 uses authenticated key establishment and AEAD; static RSA key transport removed. Used to distinguish the simplified diagram from modern TLS.

sections.title: A secret on a public network
sections.narration: Alice wants to send Bob a secret across a network Eve can watch. Encryption needs a key, but sending that key openly would defeat the whole idea. How can the first private conversation even begin?
sections.takeaway: A public network needs more than a promise that nobody is listening.

sections.title: Plaintext becomes ciphertext
sections.narration: Encryption uses a key to transform plaintext into ciphertext. The appropriate key allows recovery. Our moving blocks illustrate that change; their shapes aren't the security mechanism. Ask what information an observer would need to reverse it.
bullets: Illustrated symbols are not real crypto
sections.takeaway: Encryption conceals content through a keyed transformation.

sections.title: The algorithm can be public
sections.narration: The algorithm can be public. Security should depend on secret key material, rather than on nobody discovering the instructions. This lets a method be examined openly without giving every observer the ability to recover its messages.
bullets: Secrecy of design is not a foundation
sections.takeaway: Protect the key rather than relying on an unknown algorithm.

sections.title: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret
sections.narration: With symmetric encryption, Alice and Bob share secret key material. That shared knowledge makes protection efficient, while Eve can know the algorithm and observe ciphertext. But we've quietly assumed something important: both endpoints already possess the secret.
sections.takeaway: A symmetric key must remain secret from unauthorized parties.

sections.title: A key is not simply a memorable password
sections.narration: A cryptographic key needs suitable length and unpredictability. A short memorable phrase isn't automatically such a key, and passwords require appropriate processing. Our small key symbol represents carefully generated material, rather than an easily guessed word.
sections.takeaway: Use appropriate key generation rather than a memorable homemade key.

sections.title: The key-distribution problem
sections.narration: Now send the shared key where Eve can copy it. She gains the information needed to recover the protected message. Encryption still follows its rules; the failure came from distributing the secret that those rules relied on.
bullets: Sending K openly reveals the secret
sections.takeaway: Secure encryption still needs a sound way to establish or distribute keys.

sections.title: Give Bob a pair of keys
sections.narration: Public-key encryption changes the arrangement. Bob keeps a private key and publishes a related public key. In a suitable scheme, someone can protect information using the public key while recovery depends on Bob's private key.
sections.takeaway: A public/private key pair assigns different capabilities to each key.

sections.title: Publish the encryption key
sections.narration: Eve can read that public key too. Knowing it alone doesn't reveal the private key. But a new question appears: how does Alice establish that this public key really belongs to Bob, rather than someone pretending?
bullets: Public also does not mean trusted
sections.takeaway: Public-key distribution and public-key authentication are different problems.

sections.title: Encrypt to Bob’s public key
sections.narration: Alice has authenticated Bob's public key. She uses it to protect information for him. Eve sees the public key and ciphertext, yet lacks the private decryption capability under the scheme's assumptions. Sharing this key didn't share the secret.
bullets: Observing PK_B does not reveal SK_B
sections.takeaway: Use a suitable scheme and the intended recipient’s authenticated public key.

sections.title: Decrypt with the private key
sections.narration: Bob uses his private key to recover the protected information. The private key never needs to travel with the ciphertext. Its safe handling remains essential; public-key cryptography changes key distribution, without making private-key theft harmless.
bullets: The private key is not transmitted
sections.takeaway: Protecting private keys is part of protecting the communication.

sections.title: Why not encrypt every file this way?
sections.narration: Why not use public-key operations for every byte? Their costs and constraints make that an awkward choice for bulk data. Hybrid designs divide the work: public-key tools help establish keys, and efficient symmetric protection handles the content.
sections.takeaway: Hybrid designs combine complementary capabilities.

sections.title: Generate a fresh session key
sections.narration: Generate a fresh random session key, K. This key will protect the exchange's data rather than every unrelated conversation. Fresh key material limits reuse, while proper generation and careful protocol rules remain necessary for its protection.
bullets: Generate fresh random session key K
sections.takeaway: A hybrid example begins with appropriate session key material.

sections.title: Protect the data with the session key
sections.narration: Use K to protect the message with authenticated encryption. Alongside ciphertext comes an authentication tag, bound to the protected inputs. The scheme also defines nonce requirements and any additional information the receiver needs for verification.
sections.takeaway: Authenticated symmetric encryption protects the bulk message.

sections.title: Protect the session key for Bob
sections.narration: In this simplified model, Alice protects K with Bob's authenticated public key. That's protected key transport: securing the key that secures the data. It explains a hybrid design, rather than reproducing every step of a modern TLS handshake.
bullets: PK_B protects the small session key
This is a simplified key-transport model
sections.takeaway: Protect the session key separately from the bulk ciphertext.

sections.title: Send the two protected pieces
sections.narration: The protected key material and authenticated ciphertext now travel together. Eve can observe those packages without learning their contents under our assumptions. Encryption may still reveal metadata, including the endpoints, message sizes, and timing of the exchange.
bullets: Send protected key material and data
sections.takeaway: Ciphertext can conceal content while revealing other communication patterns.

sections.title: Bob recovers the key, then the message
sections.narration: Bob recovers K, then verifies and decrypts the data using the scheme's rules. Failed authentication means rejection. Producing something readable isn't enough; the receiver must establish that the protected message passed the required integrity check.
bullets: K authenticates and decrypts the data
sections.takeaway: A hybrid receiver verifies the protected data before accepting its contents.

sections.title: Secrecy alone does not detect tampering
sections.narration: Secrecy and integrity answer different questions. Can an observer read the message? Can an attacker change it without detection? Encryption alone doesn't automatically provide both. A suitable authenticated scheme protects the content and detects unauthorized changes.
sections.takeaway: Encryption and integrity are related but distinct security goals.

sections.title: An authentication tag checks the package
sections.narration: Change the protected message and watch verification fail. The tag isn't a checksum an attacker can recalculate after editing. Its security depends on the key and protected inputs, making unnoticed modification a different problem from accidental corruption.
bullets: A checksum is not a keyed authenticator
sections.takeaway: Authenticated encryption detects invalid protected packages.

sections.title: Do not reuse nonces carelessly
sections.narration: A nonce is an input, usually public. Many schemes require it to be unique for each use of a key. Reusing the wrong key-and-nonce pair can break protection, so its rules matter as much as the key's secrecy.
bullets: A nonce is separate from the key
sections.takeaway: Correct nonce handling is essential to secure authenticated encryption.

sections.title: A substituted public key changes everything
sections.narration: Now let Eve replace Bob's public key with her own. Alice can encrypt successfully and still protect the message for the wrong recipient. The mathematics didn't fail. The missing step was authenticating the identity behind the key.
sections.takeaway: A public key is useful only with an appropriate trust decision.

sections.title: Confidentiality is not a sender’s signature
sections.narration: There's another distinction. Anyone with Bob's public encryption key can send something he can decrypt. Successful decryption doesn't prove Alice sent it. Digital signatures use signing and verification mechanisms to address a claimed sender separately.
bullets: Encrypting for Bob does not identify Alice
sections.takeaway: Recipient confidentiality does not automatically authenticate the sender.

sections.title: How this differs from modern TLS
sections.narration: TLS version one point three commonly establishes traffic keys through authenticated ephemeral key exchange, then uses authenticated encryption. It removed static RSA key transport. Our wrapped-key picture illustrates a broader hybrid idea, rather than that exact handshake.
sections.takeaway: Use the hybrid idea to understand protocols without confusing their mechanisms.

sections.title: Use established cryptographic protocols
sections.narration: Real applications need established protocols and maintained libraries, with sound randomness and identity checks. A correct encryption operation inside a poorly designed exchange can still fail. The security comes from the whole protocol working together.
bullets: A visual analogy is not a security proof
sections.takeaway: A sound implementation must preserve the whole protocol’s security assumptions.

sections.title: Solve the secrecy puzzle
sections.narration: The opening paradox had several parts. Symmetric protection handles data; public-key tools help establish keys; authentication checks identities and protected messages. Secure communication begins when those roles fit together, rather than when one message merely looks scrambled.
bullets: Combine key setup and data protection
sections.takeaway: Secure communication combines confidentiality, integrity, and sound key handling.
